reconcile.connective: Henry distinguishes Jesus's direct reply to Pilate's own question from his silence toward the priests' accusations — the same split John's fuller dialogue reflects.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman notes Mark's Jesus speaks 'only two words' to Pilate, a contrast with John he treats as an irreconcilable trial detail.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Jesus Before the Gospels: How the Earliest Christians Remembered, Changed, and Invented Their Stories of the Savior
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus Before the Gospels (HarperOne, 2016); see also ehrmanblog.org, "The Ironies of Jesus' Trial" (Feb. 20, 2018) and "Jesus' Trial Before Pilate: Some of the Distorted Memories of the Gospels" (June 15, 2023).

excerpts.excerpt_text: These priests were very eager and noisy in their accusation; but Christ answered nothing, Mar 15:3. When Pilate urged him to clear himself, and was desirous he should (Mar 15:4), yet still he stood mute (Mar 15:5), he answered nothing, which Pilate thought very strange. He gave Pilate a direct answer (Mar 15:2), but would not answer the prosecutors and witnesses, because the things they alleged, were notoriously false, and he knew Pilate himself was convinced they were so.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly distinguishes Jesus's direct answer to Pilate's own question (paralleling John's fuller kingship dialogue) from his silence toward the chief priests' accusations (Matthew/Mark's stated silence) — the core harmonizing mechanism for this contradiction.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Mark 15:1-5
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Haley's Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible was checked directly (full-text search of the archive.org djvu transcription for "Pilate," "answered nothing," "kept silence," "not of this world," "King of the Jews," and "Am I a Jew") and returns zero hits — Haley does not treat this trial scene at all. Falling back to the contract's named alternative, Matthew Henry's own note on Mark 15:1-5 treats the passage directly, resolving the tension by distinguishing Jesus's direct reply to Pilate's personal question from his silence toward the chief priests' accusations.
